title: Check Bench
description: Add the answer back onto the number you took away, and hold the total against the number you started from.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; again, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: again, sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one pill per phase across bar, pitch 158; in user mode each is a button with a 72-tall finger box

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Find out whether a difference is right without working the same subtraction over again, by putting back what was taken away.
writeup.look: Two bays joined down the middle, the subtraction above and the check below it, with a true and false rail along the foot of the stage.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Check Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the checks written out in full against the workings standing on the bench, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one each time a total is lifted on to the shelf and the second fixed at however many workings this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The two bays stand one above the other on the left of the working area, each 700 by 206, the upper at 64,202 and the lower at 64,430, joined through the 22 tall gap between them by a spine 12 wide running down their middle. The upper bay holds the subtraction on a ruled column mat: headings across the top, the greater number on the upper row, the number taken away under it with the minus sign 40 to its left, a rule 6 tall, and the difference beneath. Drop to check slides copies of the difference and the number taken away down the spine into the lower bay, where they settle stacked with a plus sign to the left of the lower of them and a rule 6 tall under both; the originals never leave the upper bay, so the working being tested is on the stage the whole time the check is being built. The check is added column by column from the ones, each carried one drawn small above the column it goes into, and the total it builds stands under its rule in green. Hold against lifts that total out of the lower bay along a drawn path and stands it on the shelf, 300 by 206 at 826,202, beside a copy of the number the working set out from; the two are read digit for digit from the right, and the match light between them fills only when the last pair agrees and stays dark otherwise, with nothing marked either way and the first column from the right where the two part left ringed in amber. The dice bay is 300 by 206 at 826,430: it rolls five digits, builds a number from them, takes that number away from the largest five digit number and adds the two results back together on the same bench. The verdict rail runs along the foot of the working area, 1086 by 78 at 64,652, with a true end at its left and a false end at its right; a written statement is dragged to whichever end the check has earned, and a statement the check has failed springs back from the true end with the check still showing and nothing marked. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a difference or a check total is asked for, and on the third phase a pair of verdict keys reading true and false that do the same work as the rail for a child who would rather press than drag. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the greater number standing on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, the answer under the rule is green, the ten lifted out of the column on the left is vermilion, a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a column that has lent is told by the single strike through its digit and by the smaller value written small above it. Turn it round loads an addition into the upper bay in place of a subtraction, with the plus drawn where the minus stood, and the lower bay then holds a subtraction instead, so that the bench looks the same either way up and the two workings are plainly one another undone.
writeup.finish: The card shows the working the child checked, the check standing under it, and the two totals held side by side.

phases.win: the total lifts, stands beside the number on top and the match light joins them
phases.does: drops the answer and the number taken away into the bay and adds them
phases.goal: difference plus subtrahend lands on the minuend
phases.says: Put back what you took away. Where does it land?
phases.check: You have taken one number away from another and written the answer. Which two numbers do you add to get back to where you started?
phases.feels: putting back what was taken away lands on the number you set out from, every single time
phases.hands: On squared paper work 46,728 - 15,304. Then, underneath it, write the answer with the number that was taken away under it, draw a plus and a rule, and add them. Before the adding starts, ask the child to say which number on the page the total is going to land on, and then cover that number with a finger until the adding is finished.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which number was taken off the bench by the working? Second rung, the phase's: if you put that number back, what should be standing there? Third rung: the bench is cut to a two column subtraction and the child drops the pair and adds it back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the working that produced the answer is the working they know, and running it twice feels like twice the care.
wrong.move: works the subtraction a second time instead of adding anything back, because doing it again is what checking has always meant.
wrong.screen: the second subtraction runs column by column beside the first and lands on exactly the same difference, with every column agreeing. Both runs are left standing side by side, the number the working set out from stays untouched above them, and the shelf stays empty, because nothing has been built that could be stood on it.

wrong.why: the number on top is the one the check is aiming at, and the two largest numbers on the bench look like the pair that belong together.
wrong.move: adds the difference to the number on top instead of to the number that was taken away.
wrong.screen: that addition runs in the lower bay and its total is lifted to the shelf, where it stands plainly taller than the number beside it and the match light stays dark. The three rows in the upper bay are then read out by their names, and the two rows that rebuild the top one light together while the child's pair stays drawn exactly where it was put.

phases.screen: a finished subtraction above an empty check bay
phases.soWhat: Difference plus subtrahend gives the minuend back.
phases.concept: The answer and the number taken away rebuild the start

phases.win: every column of the check is filled and its total is held against the number on top
phases.does: adds the check column by column from the ones and reads the total out
phases.goal: the check is written out in columns rather than glanced at
phases.says: Write the whole check out. Looking at an answer is not checking it.
phases.check: Why is looking at a difference and deciding it seems right not the same thing as checking it?
phases.feels: the check is a sum in its own right and it has to be worked like one
phases.hands: On squared paper work 64,203 - 27,851, then write the check out underneath in full columns, carried ones drawn small above the columns they go into, with nothing done in the head at all. Ask for the check total to be read out place by place before it is compared with anything.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which column of the check has been added so far? Second rung, the phase's: which column does a check begin at? Third rung: the check is cut to two columns and the child adds those two and holds the total against the number on top. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the numbers are familiar by now and the working looked tidy while it was being done, and the bench seems to be asking for a judgement rather than for a sum.
wrong.move: looks at the two numbers, says the answer seems about right and gives a verdict without the check bay being touched.
wrong.screen: the check runs anyway at walking pace, column by column from the ones, with each column filling in green as it is added. The child's verdict stays in the answer slot the whole time, and the total the columns build is lifted to the shelf beside the number the working set out from so that the judgement and the check stand together.

wrong.why: the answer the check should reach is already printed on the stage, and the empty squares under the rule look like somewhere to put the number that is wanted.
wrong.move: writes the number from the top of the upper bay into the check's total, because that is what the check is supposed to come to.
wrong.screen: the copied total stays exactly where it was put. The check is then added column by column from the ones with every carried one drawn small above its column, and the total the columns actually build stands beside the copied one with the first column from the right where the two part lit and staying lit.

phases.screen: the check bay open with the columns empty and the plus already drawn
phases.soWhat: Write the check out in full, because glancing at an answer is not checking it.
phases.concept: A check worked all the way through

phases.win: the statement lands on the end the check earned and the true difference stands beside it
phases.does: runs the check, reads the match light and sends the statement to one end
phases.goal: a written statement is judged by the check and not by how it looks
phases.says: Somebody has written this already. Check it before you believe it.
phases.check: Somebody hands you a finished subtraction on a card. What do you do before you agree with it?
phases.feels: a wrong answer looks exactly like a right one until it has been added back
phases.hands: Have each child write a subtraction out neatly on a card and put one digit of the answer wrong on purpose, without saying where. Cards are swapped and each one is judged by adding the answer back, not by looking at it. Whoever finds a wrong card has to say what the answer should have been as well as that it was wrong.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the written answer come to when it is added back on to the number that was taken away? Second rung, the phase's: is that the number the statement started from? Third rung: the statement is cut to a two column one and the child checks it and sends it to an end. The verdict keys stay open.

wrong.why: a statement that has been written out properly looks like a statement somebody has already been through, and a tidy page is hard to doubt.
wrong.move: sends the statement to the true end because it is neatly written and its columns line up.
wrong.screen: the drag springs back from the true end with nothing marked and the statement left where it began. The check then runs of its own accord in the lower bay, adding 52,011 on to 21,340, and its total of 73,351 is lifted to the shelf beside 73,451 with the match light dark and the hundreds column, which is where the two part, left ringed in amber.

wrong.why: a verdict was what the rail asked for, and a wrong answer feels finished the moment it has been called wrong.
wrong.move: sends the statement to the false end and moves on without ever working out what it should have said.
wrong.screen: the statement stays at the false end where the child put it. The working in the upper bay is then opened again column by column from the ones until it builds 52,111, that difference is dropped into the check bay and added on to 21,340, and the total is lifted to the shelf, where it lands on 73,451 and the match light fills.

phases.screen: a statement already written out, with the verdict rail waiting below it
phases.soWhat: Check a written answer before you believe it, and then say what it should have been.
phases.concept: A printed answer can be wrong

phases.win: the other number is left exactly, and the two bays read as one another undone
phases.does: takes one of the two numbers from the total and looks for the other
phases.goal: an addition can be tested by taking one of its numbers away
phases.says: This time it is an addition. How would taking away test it?
phases.check: You have added two numbers together. How could taking away tell you whether the total is right?
phases.feels: the two workings undo each other, so either one can be used to test the other
phases.hands: Write 27,415 + 36,208 on squared paper and add it. Then, without adding anything again, take 36,208 away from the total and see which number is left. Do it once more taking the other number away instead. Finish with the dice game in threes, where a rolled number is taken from 99,999 and the two results are added back together.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of the three numbers is the total? Second rung, the phase's: what should be left when one part is taken off the total? Third rung: the bench is cut to a two column addition and the child checks it by taking one number away. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: adding is the working in front of them, and checking has meant doing the same thing again for as long as they have been checking anything.
wrong.move: adds the two numbers together a second time to check the addition.
wrong.screen: the second addition runs beside the first and lands on the same total, column for column and carry for carry, with both runs left standing. The turn it round control then lights on its own, and the lower bay opens with a minus drawn in it and one of the two numbers already waiting underneath the total.

wrong.why: subtraction has always begun from the biggest number on the page, and a total reads as something that was made rather than as a number to work from.
wrong.move: takes the smaller of the two numbers away from the greater one instead of taking either of them away from the total.
wrong.screen: that subtraction runs in the lower bay and leaves 8,793, which is none of the three numbers on the bench, and it is left standing. The three numbers are then named out loud as two parts and a total with the total lit, the check is laid again taking one part away from the total, and both runs stay on the stage together.

phases.screen: an addition handed over in the upper bay with the turn it round control lit
phases.soWhat: To check an addition, take one of its two numbers away from the total and look for the other one.
phases.concept: Addition and subtraction check each other

writeup.delight: The moment hold against is pressed. The total lifts out of the lower bay and travels up the drawn path to the shelf, where it comes to rest beside the number the working set out from. The two are then read off digit for digit from the right, one pair at a time, with each pair lighting as it is read, and the match light between them fills only once the last pair on the left has agreed. Where they part, the reading stops at the first column from the right that parts them, that column keeps a small amber ring, and the light stays dark with nothing else marked anywhere.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a finished subtraction stands in the upper bay with its difference under the rule, and the lower bay is empty with its plus sign already drawn and its columns blank. On the second the two numbers of the check have come down into the lower bay and are stacked with a rule beneath them, every square under that rule still empty. On the third a written statement lies across the middle of the stage, already worked out by somebody else, with the verdict rail waiting along the foot and both of its ends dark. On the fourth an addition sits in the upper bay instead of a subtraction, with the turn it round control lit beside it. The running count at the top left holds the checks written out against the workings on the bench, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the difference under the rule, or the first empty column of the check, or the written statement, or the total of the addition, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what putting back what was taken away would land on. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any subtraction, with the check bay, the verdict rail and the dice bay all open at once. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on adding the answer back, writing the check out in full, judging a written statement, and checking an addition by taking one number away.
voiceLines: Two bays. The working in the upper one, and the putting back in the lower one.
Put back what you took away. Where does it land?
Write the whole check out. Looking at an answer is not checking it.
Somebody has written this already. Check it before you believe it.
This time it is an addition. How would taking away test it?
Another working. Put back what was taken away and see where it lands.
Free play. Any subtraction, the verdict rail live and the dice bay open beside it.
Send them down again and add the whole check out, column by column.
Every check written out in full, and every total held against the number it set out from.

observations.why: Working the same subtraction over again repeats whatever produced the answer the first time.
observations.soWhat: A check that repeats the working is not a check, however carefully it is done.
observations.observe: The check was a different sum from the one it was testing, and that is the only reason it caught anything.

observations.why: Two numbers can only be read against each other properly while both of them are showing.
observations.soWhat: The check and the number it is being tested against belong in the same frame.
observations.observe: The total the check built was stood beside the number the working set out from, not compared from memory.

observations.why: The check adds the whole thing at one go, so it tests the answer and not any single step inside it.
observations.soWhat: A failed check sends you back to the working; it does not hand you the mistake.
observations.observe: When the check failed it said that the working was wrong and never once said which column was wrong.

observations.why: Nothing about the way a number is written down says anything about whether it is true.
observations.soWhat: A printed answer earns belief by being checked, and by nothing else.
observations.observe: A written statement that was wrong looked exactly like one that was right.

phases.screen: a finished subtraction above an empty check bay

phases.traceback: The pair drops into the lower bay and is added column by column from the ones, each carry small above its column; the total lifts to the shelf, the lid opens on the start, the pairs are read from the right and the match light fills. When the number on top was added instead, that sum runs first and stands taller than the start with the light dark, the rows are named, and the right pair rebuilds the start.

phases.traceback: The child's answer drops into the lower bay and is added back column by column; its total stands on the shelf beside the number on top with the light dark and the first column that parts ringed; then the subtraction is worked again column by column, a ten taken where the top is short, and the right answer is checked until the light fills.
ladder: Add your answer back onto the number taken away. Does it make the number on top?
Which column of the check has been added so far?

phases.win: the statement lands on the end the check earned and the true difference stands beside it

ladder: What does the written answer come to when it is added back on to the number that was taken away?
Add the written answer back. Does the total match the number the board started at?
Hold its check against the start. Do the two read the same?

phases.screen: an addition handed over in the upper bay with the turn it round control lit
phases.win: the other number is left exactly, and the two bays read as one another undone
phases.traceback: The bench turns round and the part is taken from the total column by column from the ones, each trade a struck digit with its new value small above in rose; what is left lifts to the shelf, the lid opens on the other part and the light fills. The dice sum is added back column by column and held against 99,999, where the hundreds part.

Start from the total, not from the two parts. What is left after taking one away?

bays.rows: the number on top, the number taken away with its sign 76 to the left, a rule 6 tall, the answer in one square a column

shelf.matchLight: fills only when the last pair from the right agrees; the first pair that parts keeps an amber ring

diceBay.use: phase 4 question 3 and free play: five dice build the number taken from 99,999

model.lid: the number a check should land on (the start in phase 1, the other part in phase 4) waits under a lid until the check is held against it
model.runs: checks held against the start in this phase, and the sums on the bench (3)

freePlay.first: the chapter's worked check, 98,975 take away 56,986
freePlay.dice: Roll: five dice, 1 to 6, make the number taken from 99,999
freePlay.slip: puts a one-column slip into the working so the check can catch it
freePlay.rail: the statement card docks at either end
freePlay.check: drop the answer down: it is added back and held against 99,999 by itself

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The pair drops into the lower bay and is added column by column from the ones, each carry small above its column; the total lifts to the shelf, the lid opens on the start, the pairs are read from the right and the match light fills. When the number on top was added instead, that sum runs first and stands taller than the start with the light dark, the rows are named, and the right pair rebuilds the start.

Phase 2: The child's answer drops into the lower bay and is added back column by column; its total stands on the shelf beside the number on top with the light dark and the first column that parts ringed; then the subtraction is worked again column by column, a ten taken where the top is short, and the right answer is checked until the light fills.

Phase 3: The statement springs back to the middle of the rail with nothing marked; the check runs by itself (drop, add it back, hold it against the start), the pairs are read from the right, and the end the check earned lights, with the true difference beside it when the statement fails.

Phase 4: The bench turns round and the part is taken from the total column by column from the ones, each trade a struck digit with its new value small above in rose; what is left lifts to the shelf, the lid opens on the other part and the light fills. The dice sum is added back column by column and held against 99,999, where the hundreds part.

voice.opening: Two bays. The working in the upper one, and the putting back in the lower one.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every check written out in full, and every total held against the number it set out from.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: Take 21,543 from 53,959, then add your answer back onto 21,543. Where does it land?

question.en: The working took 21,543 away. It left 32,416. The start is under the lid. Drop them down and add them back together.

items.planAnswer: On 53,959, the number the working started from

items.planQuestion: A difference is 5,214 and the subtrahend is 3,478. What was the number on top?

question.en: The difference is 5,214. The subtrahend is 3,478. What was the number on top?

items.planQuestion: What do you add to a difference to get back to the number the working started from?

question.en: What do you add to a difference to get back to the number the working started from? Drag it down beside the answer.

items.planAnswer: The subtrahend, which is the number that was taken away

items.planQuestion: Subtract 46,208 from 81,375 and write the check out in full.

question.en: Start at 81,375. Take away 46,208. Type what is left, then write the check out in full.

items.planQuestion: Subtract 12,304 from 29,857 and check the answer by addition.

question.en: Start at 29,857. Take away 12,304. Then check the answer by addition.

items.planQuestion: The difference between two numbers is 3,946 and the greater number is 8,120. Find the smaller number and check it.

question.en: The greater number is 8,120. The difference is 3,946. Find the smaller number and check it.

items.planQuestion: A sheet has 47,382 - 25,140 = 21,242 already written on it. Check it and say whether it holds.

question.en: A sheet starts at 47,382. It takes away 25,140. It writes 21,242. Check it, then say whether it holds.

items.planAnswer: It is wrong. The true difference is 22,242

items.planQuestion: A board reads 63,470 - 41,250 = 22,120. Is the statement right?

question.en: A board starts at 63,470. It takes away 41,250. It writes 22,120. Is the statement right?

items.planAnswer: No. The true difference is 22,220, because 22,220 + 41,250 = 63,470

items.planQuestion: A board reads 58,916 - 27,504 = 31,412. Is the statement right?

question.en: A board starts at 58,916. It takes away 27,504. It writes 31,412. True or false?

items.planAnswer: Yes. Adding 31,412 and 27,504 gives 58,916, the number it started from

items.planQuestion: A child adds 34,506 and 28,197 and gets 62,703. Use subtraction to check it.

question.en: A child adds two numbers and gets 62,703. One of them is 28,197. The other is under the lid. Turn it round. Take 28,197 from the total.

items.planQuestion: A shopkeeper adds 25,634 and 19,087 and writes 44,721. Check the total by taking one number away.

question.en: A shopkeeper writes 44,721 as a total. One of the two numbers is 19,087. The lid hides the other. Take 19,087 away to check it.

items.planQuestion: In a game of three, a rolled number of 12,345 is taken from 99,999 and the answer is written as 87,554. Add it back and say whether it holds.

question.en: In a game of three, the dice make 12,345. It is taken from 99,999. The answer is written as 87,554. Add it back. Does it hold?

items.planAnswer: It is wrong. Adding 87,554 and 12,345 gives 99,899, not 99,999, so the difference should be 87,654

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

voiceLines.en: Two bays. The working in the upper one, and the putting back in the lower one.
Put back what you took away. Where does it land?
Write the whole check out. Looking at an answer is not checking it.
Somebody has written this already. Check it before you believe it.
This time it is an addition. How would taking away test it?
Another working. Put back what was taken away and see where it lands.
Free play. Any subtraction, the verdict rail live and the dice bay open beside it.
Send them down again and add the whole check out, column by column.
Every check written out in full, and every total held against the number it set out from.
